title: What prayer is (CCC 2559–2565)

cards: A well in Samaria, outside a town, and a stranger sitting on its edge, tired from walking. A woman comes out with her jar, around the sixth hour, the Gospel says. And the stranger speaks first.
Not with a sermon. With a request. "Give me to drink."
At the start of its fourth part, on prayer, the Catechism goes to that well. Before it says anything about how to pray, it notices who asked first.

teach.b: At the end of year one, you met prayer as a relationship. Here is the Catechism's fuller picture, in three words: gift, covenant, communion. First, gift.

It quotes Thérèse of Lisieux: prayer is a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven, a cry of thanks and of love in trial as in joy. And John Damascene: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God.
Then something humbling: we don't know how to pray as we ought, so humility is where prayer begins. Which brings it to the well.
In John's Gospel, Jesus tells the woman, "If thou didst know the gift of God," she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water.
The Catechism reads the scene this way: it is Jesus who is thirsty, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Then Augustine: God thirsts that we may thirst for him.
Whether we know it or not, prayer is the meeting of two thirsts. Second, covenant.
Prayer comes from the heart, the hidden center of a person, the place of decision and of truth, where we choose life or death.
And it's a covenant because it's a relationship God started, binding him and us together in Christ.
Third, communion: the living relationship of God's children with their Father, with his Son Jesus Christ, and with the Holy Spirit. Not a technique. A life with someone.
Before a single instruction, then, the Catechism says: you're not the one who started this.

how: Catholics pray in many ways, alone and together, aloud and in silence; the Catechism opens its teaching on prayer by calling it a gift from God, a covenant relationship and a communion with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

games.q: a woman comes to a well around the sixth hour. a tired stranger is sitting there. who speaks first, and what does he say?
o: she does: she asks who he is.
he does: he asks her for a drink.
nobody: she fills her jar and leaves.
games.why: Jesus speaks first: "Give me to drink." the Catechism reads it as God's thirst for us coming before our prayer.

practice: Don't try to say anything yet; picture the well, the heat, the jar, and the stranger who asks first, and notice your own thirst today, for rest, for peace, for someone to listen.
If you pray, simply turn toward God, the way Thérèse put it, a simple look; if you don't, stay with the thirst without fixing it.
